report:
## Conclusion: Yes — the evidence strongly supports that denosumab reduces vertebral fracture risk in osteoporosis, though this benefit is contingent on continued treatment.

**Primary evidence:** The pivotal FREEDOM trial, a large randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, found that denosumab given subcutaneously every 6 months for 36 months significantly reduced the risk of new vertebral fractures, as well as nonvertebral and hip fractures, compared with placebo (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493). This is considered the definitive efficacy trial supporting the drug's approval.

**Long-term confirmation:** The 10-year FREEDOM Extension study confirmed that continued denosumab use is associated with sustained low rates of vertebral fracture and progressive bone mineral density gains, without a plateau, supporting durable efficacy (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/landia/article/PIIS2213-8587(17)30138-9/fulltext).

**Important caveat — discontinuation risk:** A critical body of evidence shows that stopping denosumab causes a "rebound" effect: rapid loss of bone density gains and a rebound increase in bone turnover, which can lead to an increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures, sometimes occurring in clusters shortly after the last dose. A post hoc analysis of FREEDOM and its extension specifically documented this elevated risk after discontinuation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5915244/).

**Comparative evidence (mixed):** Some meta-analyses suggest denosumab may reduce fractures more than bisphosphonates, but results are not fully conclusive, and at least one meta-analysis found no significant fracture-reduction advantage over bisphosphonates (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6447951/).

**Bottom line:** Denosumab robustly reduces vertebral fracture risk during active treatment, but discontinuation without transition therapy can reverse this benefit and even increase fracture risk.
